name: Bandwagon effect
statement: People want a thing more because other people already want it, so popularity feeds on itself and early advantages harden into lasting ones.
meaning: The name covers three claims that are usually run together. The economic one is that an individual's demand for a good rises with the number of other people buying it, which makes the market demand curve something other than the sum of the individual ones. The political one is that published poll results move voters towards whoever is ahead. The third, and the one with the best evidence, is that visible counts of other people's choices, downloads, up-votes, signatures, ratings, change what later arrivals choose. Only the third has been tested by randomly assigning the popularity signal itself, which is what separates influence from shared taste.

origin.note: Leibenstein defined the bandwagon effect as "the extent to which the demand for a commodity is increased due to the fact that others are also consuming the same commodity", one of three kinds of nonfunctional demand alongside the snob and Veblen effects. The paper is pure demand theory with diagrams and no data, prompted by Oskar Morgenstern's 1948 argument that collective demand curves are not additive. The political usage runs on a separate track: Herbert Simon paired bandwagon and underdog effects in the title of a 1954 paper in Public Opinion Quarterly.

evidence: The load-bearing studies are web experiments that manipulated the popularity signal directly. Salganik, Dodds and Watts built an artificial music market with 14,341 participants and 48 songs by unknown bands. Arrivals were assigned either to an independent condition, which showed song and band names only, or to a social influence condition, which also showed download counts. Social influence participants were split across eight parallel worlds that could not see each other. In both of the two experiments run, all eight social influence worlds had a higher Gini coefficient of download share than the single independent world, and the same song varied more in market share between worlds than between random halves of the independent condition, with P < 0.01. Raising the salience of the signal, by listing songs in descending order of downloads rather than in a random grid, raised inequality and unpredictability further. The best songs rarely did badly and the worst rarely did well, and almost anything else happened. Salganik and Watts then inverted the displayed download counts for 12,207 participants and found that most songs' falsely reported popularity became real, though the best songs recovered in the long run. Muchnik, Aral and Taylor moved the design onto a live social news site, randomly assigning 101,281 comments over five months to a first up-vote, a first down-vote or nothing. To match the site's natural rates, 4,049 were up-treated and 1,942 down-treated. Those comments were viewed more than 10 million times and rated 308,515 times. The up-vote raised the chance that the first viewer also up-voted by 32% over control, and the final mean score of up-treated comments ran 25% above control. Up-treated comments were 30% more likely to reach a score of 10, 6.4% against 4.9%. The down-vote behaved differently. It raised the chance of a further down-vote from 0.007 to 0.014, and that was swamped by correction: the chance of a down-treated comment being up-voted was 0.099 against 0.054 for control, and the final mean scores of down-treated comments were not statistically different from control. Positive herding that accumulates against negative herding that gets corrected is the paper's headline finding.

replication.headline: The manipulated-popularity experiments repeat in new media and on new platforms. Whether the up-vote and the down-vote work asymmetrically depends on the site, and the claim that polls push voters towards the leader does not repeat reliably.
replication.detail: Epstein, Groh, Dubey and Pentland re-ran the music market design on a platform where people curate AI-generated hybrid animals, randomising both the social signal and the visual layout. They report that they replicate the original finding of an unpredictable winner-take-all market, and add that social influence also produced local trends more diverse than the baseline. Van de Rijt and colleagues took the same logic into four live systems at once, giving arbitrary early success to randomly chosen recipients. Subsequent success rose in every one: 70% against 39% for funded Kickstarter projects, 90% against 77% for helpfully rated reviews on Epinions, 40% against 31% for Wikipedia status awards, and 66% against 52% for Change.org petitions. The gaps persisted but did not compound, since larger initial advantages produced little further separation. Glenski and Weninger ran the same kind of vote manipulation on Reddit for six months, treating 93,019 posts and 96,486 comments. The result splits. Positive treatment raised the final rating of posts by 11.02% but did nothing for comments, and, against Muchnik and colleagues, negative treatment lowered final ratings of posts by 5.15% and of comments by 37.4%. Positive treatment raised a post's chance of reaching a score of 2,000 by 24.6%, and negative treatment cut a comment's chance of the same by 46.6%. So the correction Muchnik and colleagues found for down-votes did not appear on Reddit. Cicognani, Figini and Magnani carried the question to hotel guests, manipulating which prior ratings a guest saw before reviewing a stay. Their abstract reports the asymmetry: ratings above the hotel's average raised the guest's own rating, ratings below it did not move it. Guests new to the hotel, and guests who rarely write reviews, were the more susceptible. The polling literature is where the disagreement sits. Farjam had 1,113 participants allocate a budget among real political organisations and found the most popular option gained about 7% of votes once poll results were shown, with no underdog effect. Van der Meer, Hakhverdian and Aaldering, with 23,421 Dutch respondents, found that poll standings alone moved no vote intentions, and that only an emphasis on a party's growth in the polls raised support. Undecided voters were not more susceptible.

study.cite: Epstein, Z., Groh, M., Dubey, A., & Pentland, A. (2021). Social influence leads to the formation of diverse local trends. Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction, 5(CSCW2), 1-18.

limits: Two reanalyses qualify what the music market showed. Krumme, Cebrian, Pickard and Pentland split the participant's decision in two, whether to sample a song and whether to download it once heard, and report that social influence bears on the first step only. Ormerod and Glass attack the unpredictability reading from the other side. Using the ratio of mean to median downloads as a trigger, they found that in four of the worlds the eventual winner was already the outright leader when it held between 7 and 13 downloads, between 4.11% and 5.31% of the way through the downloads, and in five more it was among a group of two to six joint leaders that early. Their claim is that unpredictability before the process starts is compatible with the winner being identifiable soon after it does. Leibenstein's paper is a theoretical construction and tests nothing, so the demand-curve claim does not inherit the evidence from the web experiments. Those experiments show that a manipulated popularity signal changes later choices among options the participant has no strong prior view about: unknown songs, unfamiliar comments, machine-generated pictures. Nothing in them speaks to whether the same holds for well-known brands or long-held political loyalties. The herding results are also platform-specific in ways their authors flag, and Muchnik and colleagues found the effect only for comments filed under politics, culture and society, and business, not under economics, IT, fun or general news. Van de Rijt and colleagues report decreasing marginal returns, which cuts against the runaway version of the story. No meta-analysis of poll-induced bandwagon effects on vote choice was located, in Crossref searches or in the reference lists of the papers read here. The only bandwagon meta-analysis found, by Wang, Chu and Huang across 161 effect sizes from 41 studies, is about credibility perceptions rather than voting, and reports a positive but small effect. The Cicognani, Figini and Magnani article stayed behind a paywall on this pass, so its design and its asymmetry are described from the published abstract and no figure from it appears above. Searches for a critique or a reanalysis of the Muchnik experiment itself covered Crossref, Semantic Scholar and open-web searching, and turned up replications on other platforms rather than any published challenge to that paper's analysis.
misreadings: The three literatures get quoted as one body of evidence, and they are not. A reader who cites Leibenstein for the proposition that up-votes distort ratings is citing a 1950 diagram. Muchnik and colleagues' 25% is the gap in mean final comment score between treated and control comments on one website, not a general figure for how much any crowd rating is inflated. Their asymmetry is quoted as though a down-vote does nothing, and what they report is a down-vote that raises later down-voting and is then overtaken by users up-voting to correct it. These platform experiments are also not laboratory conformity. Asch put a person in front of a unanimous group and measured whether they would say aloud something they could see was false; these studies alter a number on a screen and count a later click. The two literatures share a word and little else. The reverse is documented as well as the forward direction: Ceci and Kain found poll information shifted both attitude strength and candidate preference, explained it as oppositional reactivity, and Chatterjee and Kamal, using India's 2009 ban on publishing exit polls, found that frontrunners gained vote share once the polls went dark, which points to underdog voting when they were visible. Leibenstein himself defined the mirror image in economics as the snob effect, where demand falls as others buy. Barnfield's review of the political science literature argues the term is used for several distinct phenomena at once, and that studies claiming to find or refute a bandwagon effect are often not testing the same thing.
